sub: From snowflakes to flavors, eight units reveal a God who is not only mighty in power but beautiful and good.

units.title: Snowflakes: No Two Alike
units.sub: Tiny six-pointed messengers falling from heaven, each one a one-of-a-kind work of art.

share.v: He gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes.

blocks.h: Under a magnifying glass, a snowflake looks like a finely carved six-pointed star: six arms, each sprouting delicate branches and patterns. It lasts only a few seconds before melting in your palm.

Wilson Bentley, a farmer in Vermont, fell in love with snowflakes as a boy. On January 15, 1885, he became the first person to photograph a snowflake through a microscope with a camera, and over his lifetime he took more than 5,000 pictures. Late in life he co-authored the book Snow Crystals with the meteorologist W. J. Humphreys.
Out of whose womb came the ice? The gray frost of the sky, who has given birth to it?
Why are snowflakes six-sided?

items: How the molecules line up: when water freezes, its molecules link through hydrogen bonds into a hexagonal lattice. A snowflake's sixfold symmetry is that tiny lattice scaled up until our eyes can see it.
Temperature sets the shape: at about −2 °C crystals grow as thin plates; at about −5 °C as columns and fine needles; at about −15 °C they grow the most beautiful branching stars.
Humidity sets the pattern: the more water vapor in the air, the faster the arms grow and the more they branch.

blocks.h: A snowflake is like a diary. As it falls from the cloud, it passes through different temperatures and humidities, and each stage of the journey writes a line on its arms. All six arms travel the same journey at the same time, so they write almost the same words; and since no two snowflakes travel exactly the same path, no two diaries are the same.

In 1936 the Japanese physicist Ukichiro Nakaya became the first to grow artificial snow crystals in the laboratory. He charted how temperature and water vapor relate to crystal shape, a chart later called the "Nakaya diagram." He left us a famous saying: "Snow crystals are letters sent from heaven."

The physicist Kenneth Libbrecht points out that a single snowflake contains more than 1018 water molecules, and the possible arrangements of a complex branching snowflake are unimaginably many, so the chance of two being exactly alike is practically zero. Simple little columnar crystals just forming in a cloud, however, can look very similar; in 1988 a researcher reported finding two small crystals that looked almost identical.
A snowflake's sixfold symmetry comes from the hexagonal structure of the ice lattice; its outward shape is determined mainly by temperature and water-vapor supersaturation.
Bentley first photographed a snowflake through a microscope in 1885 and left more than five thousand images over his lifetime.
"No two snowflakes are alike" is almost certainly true for complex branching snowflakes; but small, simply shaped crystals can look very similar, so the saying needs a qualification.

A snowflake's beauty far exceeds what its existence "requires." This kind of beauty, exquisite even when no one is watching, points to a Creator who delights in making beautiful things. This is a philosophical inference.
His beauty: lovely even where no one sees

Every year countless snowflakes fall into empty valleys. No one ever glances at them, yet they are just as exquisite. God creates beauty not for applause, but because He Himself is beautiful and good.
He gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes.
Every snowflake is one of a kind, and so are you. God knows every snowflake, and He knows your name and your story even better.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
The next time you see snow, frost, or ice patterns on a window (or a snowflake photo online), stop and look closely for thirty seconds.
Reflect: Do I often feel ordinary and replaceable? God never makes the same snowflake twice. How does He see me?

Prayer: Lord who made the snowflakes, thank You for so carefully making me one of a kind. Take away my heart of comparing myself with others, and help me live before You as the person You made me to be. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: my worth is not decided by what others think of me but by God's Word: I am His wonderful work.
Humility overcomes pride: no need to envy someone else's shape, and no need to look down on my own; return to our proper place, letting God be God and letting me be me.
People matter more than tasks: everyone around me is God's unique handiwork; replace comparison with appreciation.

blocks.h: This week: write down three unique things God has placed in you, and affirm, face to face, what is unique about a family member or friend.
Quiz

quiz.q: Why are most snowflakes six-sided?
o: Because clouds are hexagonal
Because water molecules form a hexagonal lattice when they freeze
Because snowflakes spin in the air
quiz.e: Ice has a hexagonal lattice, and a snowflake's sixfold symmetry is that structure magnified.

quiz.q: What mainly decides whether a snow crystal grows as a plate or a column?
o: Temperature
Wind speed
How long it takes to land
quiz.e: Ukichiro Nakaya found that temperature sets the basic shape, while the amount of water vapor sets how elaborate the branching becomes.

quiz.q: Which statement about "no two snowflakes are alike" is most accurate?
o: Completely false; snowflakes are often identical
Complex snowflakes are almost never identical, but small simple crystals can look very alike
Every snowflake has the same number of molecules
quiz.e: Complex branching snowflakes have unimaginably many possible arrangements; small simple crystals can look nearly identical.

units.title: The Peacock and Structural Color
units.sub: Not a single drop of blue pigment, yet it blazes with the brightest blue-green.

share.v: One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple.

blocks.h: When a peacock spreads his train, hundreds of "eyespots" shimmer in blue, green, gold, and bronze. Shift your viewing angle, and the colors shift with you.
Here is the amazing part: if you ground a peacock feather into powder, you would not get a pile of blue-green dust. Those colors are not in any "paint" at all.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches.
Not pigment, but structure

items: Pigment color: in carrots or leaves, molecules absorb certain colors of light and reflect the rest.

Structural color: the material itself may be brown or clear, but it is arranged in regular structures smaller than a wavelength of light, so certain colors reinforce one another while others cancel out.
Color that changes with angle: this "iridescence" is the signature of structural color.

blocks.h: Structural color is like a soap bubble. Soapy water has no color of its own, but when the film's thickness is close to the wavelength of light, it shows rainbow colors. A peacock feather holds thousands upon thousands of such precise "films."

Using electron microscopes, Jian Zi of Fudan University and colleagues found that in the outer layer of a peacock's barbules, tiny melanin rods are embedded in keratin and arranged in a regular two-dimensional lattice, a natural "photonic crystal." Different lattice spacings give different colors: blue has a spacing of about 140 nanometers, green and yellow slightly larger; brown comes from fewer layers combined with other effects.

In 1860 Darwin wrote to the American botanist Asa Gray that the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail, whenever he gazed at it, made him "sick," because such splendor was hard to explain as "useful for survival." Later, in The Descent of Man, he proposed sexual selection: the peahen's preferences shaped the peacock's train.

items.h: Over time, females preferred more splendid males, so splendid traits were preserved and enhanced. This is the mainstream biological explanation, though the details of which preferences, and why, are still debated.

Even if we accept the mechanism of sexual selection, we can still ask: why do the laws of physics allow such exquisite structures as photonic crystals? Why can animals and humans perceive beauty at all? These are questions at the level of philosophy.

blocks.h: The blue-green of peacock feathers is mainly structural color, produced by regular nanostructures of melanin rods arranged in keratin.
The color of a structural color is set by the spacing of the structure, which is why it changes with viewing angle.
The evolution of the peacock's train is mainly explained by sexual selection, but studies disagree on exactly what peahens base their choice on.
"Painting" color with nanometer-scale precision is craftsmanship so ingenious that it brings to mind a wise Designer who loves beauty. This is a philosophical inference.
His beauty: beauty flows from who He is
What David wanted most in life was not wealth but "to see Yahweh's beauty." The peacock's beauty is only a shadow; God Himself is Beauty itself.
One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple.
A peacock's color is not in dye on the surface but in the structure within. God looks at people the same way: not at the outer packaging, but at the heart.
For I don't see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.
Find a photo of a peacock feather, or a real one, and watch how its colors change from different angles.
Reflect: How much effort do I spend on the outer "paint"? And how much do I spend letting God build the "structure" within me?
Prayer: Beautiful Lord, I want to gaze on Your beauty all my life. Change me from the inside out, so that my life naturally reflects Your splendor. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Life first, then relationships, then ministry: color comes from inner structure; the fruit of ministry also comes from inner life.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: the peacock does not shine for itself; it reflects the light that falls on it.
Changing our mindset: from looking at the outside to looking at the heart, from man's point of view to God's point of view.

blocks.h: This week: spend ten quiet minutes each day reading Scripture and praying, focused on "seeing His beauty," and let God build up the life within you.
Quiz

quiz.q: If you grind a blue peacock feather into powder, what color do you see?
o: Bright blue
Shimmering green
Mostly dark brown, because the color comes from structure, not pigment
quiz.e: Once the structure is destroyed, the interference effect disappears, leaving only the dark color of the melanin.

quiz.q: Which of these works most like structural color?
o: The colors on a soap bubble
The color of a crayon
The orange of a carrot
quiz.e: A soap bubble shows thin-film interference, similar in principle to the structural color of peacock feathers.

quiz.q: In Psalm 27:4, what did David seek all his life?
o: More wealth
To see Yahweh's beauty
To defeat his enemies
quiz.e: "That I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty."

units.title: The Butterfly's Wings
units.sub: Tens of thousands of tiny scales pieced together into flying stained glass.

share.v: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

blocks.h: Touch a butterfly's wing with your finger, and a fine powder comes off on your fingertip. That is not dust; it is thousands of tiny scales.
The order that butterflies and moths belong to, Lepidoptera, gets its name from the Greek words for "scale" and "wing."
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts.
A picture made of scales

items: Laid like roof tiles: row upon row of scales overlap on the wing's clear membrane.
One scale, one color: the patterns on a wing are pieced together like a mosaic from many single-colored scales.
Two ways to color: some scales contain pigment; some produce structural color through fine microstructures; some use both.

blocks.h: A butterfly's wing is like a mosaic mural made of tiny tiles. From a distance you see a complete picture; up close you discover that each "tile" is so small you need a microscope to see it clearly.
The blue of the Morpho

The wings of the Morpho butterflies of Central and South America are a dazzling blue that flashes in the sunlight as the angle changes. Their scales carry lengthwise ridges, and the sides of each ridge bear several extremely thin layers, like rows of tiny Christmas trees. These layers alternate with air, so blue light reinforces itself.

A team led by the British physicist Pete Vukusic measured single Morpho scales and found that some structures can reflect as much as about 75% of incoming blue light, across a very wide range of angles. These structures have also inspired research into anti-counterfeiting, sensors, and more.
A butterfly's wing color comes from its scales; some scale colors come from pigments, others from nanostructures.
The Morpho's blue is structural color, caused by light interference from multiple layers alternating with air on the scale ridges.
How these delicate structures are precisely "assembled" during development is still an active area of research.

An insect's wing serves flight, warmth, and recognition of its own kind, and is stunningly beautiful all at once. Many see this many-sided fittingness as a clue to design. This is a philosophical inference.
His beauty: from caterpillar to butterfly
The butterfly's beauty comes through a complete transformation. Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is reorganized, and it emerges as something entirely new.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
The Bible says that as we behold the Lord's glory, we are gradually transformed into His image. This is not something we squeeze out by our own effort; it is the Holy Spirit's work within us.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.
Think back to your life before you believed and your life now. What has God already changed in you?
Reflect: What part of my life is still like a "caterpillar," needing to be handed over to God to be reshaped in the "chrysalis"?

Prayer: Lord who makes us new creations, thank You for not giving up on me. I hand my old ways over to You. Holy Spirit, renew me day by day, so that I go from glory to glory and become more like Jesus. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Holy Spirit is my guide: transformation comes "from the Lord, the Spirit"; I ask the Holy Spirit to renew me daily.
The eight steps of changing our mindset: information, revelation, conviction, practice... change takes a process, and it takes repetition.
Selflessness: it is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me; only when the old self steps aside can the new life spread its wings.

blocks.h: This week: pick one old habit you want to change, write down one concrete new practice, and ask a spiritual companion to pray for you and check in with you every week.
Quiz

quiz.q: What does the name "Lepidoptera" mean?
o: Scaled wings
Color-changing insects
Flower-loving insects
quiz.e: Lepidoptera is formed from the Greek words for "scale" and "wing."

quiz.q: What mainly produces the Morpho's blue?
o: Blue pigment
Light interference from multilayered structures on the scales
A reflection of the sky
quiz.e: It is structural color, produced by the fine arrangement of ridges and layers on the scales.

quiz.q: According to 2 Corinthians 3:18, how are we "transformed into the same image"?
o: By our own effort
By other people's praise
By seeing the glory of the Lord, transformed by the Lord, the Spirit
quiz.e: The source of transformation is the Holy Spirit; our part is to look to the Lord with unveiled face.

units.title: Birdsong and Music
units.sub: Birdsong in the morning light and the song in the human heart both invite us to praise.

share.v: Let everything that has breath praise Yah! Praise Yah!

blocks.h: Before dawn, the birds outside the window begin to sing. One after another, like a morning choir with no conductor.
Many songbirds are not born knowing their songs. They learn by listening to adult birds when young and practicing again and again, just as children learn to talk.
The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
The structure of birdsong

items: Organized: birdsong is built from notes into phrases, and from phrases into complete songs, with a fixed order and rhythm.
Learned: many young songbirds have a learning period in which they must listen, imitate, and practice before they sing like adults.
A special voice box: a songbird's syrinx has two sound sources, left and right, so it can produce two different notes at the same time.
Purposeful: birdsong is used mainly to claim territory and attract a mate.

blocks.h: A young bird learning to sing is like a child learning piano: first listening to the teacher play, then trying it again and again, going from tuneless to gradually fluent. Birds that never hear a teacher often cannot sing a complete song.

Researchers analyzing the song of the North American hermit thrush found that most of the pitches it chooses fall on the "harmonic series" of a single fundamental, the same simple whole-number ratios behind human musical scales. This was the first time the phenomenon was demonstrated in an animal with rigorous statistical methods.

On the human side, a Harvard team analyzing a large body of ethnographic data found music in every society they studied; lullabies, dance songs, and the like share similar features across cultures. Brain-imaging studies have also found that when music moves us to "goosebumps," the brain's reward system becomes active and releases dopamine.
Many songbirds can learn their songs only by hearing adult models and practicing when young.
The hermit thrush's pitch choices match the harmonic series; scholars still interpret differently whether this means birds have a "musical sense."
Music is present in every human society; intense musical emotion is linked with activity in the brain's reward system.
Humans everywhere create and enjoy music far beyond what survival requires, which fits the biblical view that people were made for praise. This is a philosophical inference.
His goodness: God Himself sings
The Bible is full of songs from beginning to end: creation is called to praise, God's people are called to sing, and God Himself even rejoices over His people with singing.
Yahweh, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.
The birds don't know whom they are praising, but we can know. Praise is giving the voices of creation back to the Lord who made every voice.
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live. I will sing praise to my God while I have any being.
Tomorrow morning, open a window or step outside, listen quietly to the birds for one minute, and then sing a hymn or worship song you love.
Reflect: Is my mouth used mostly for complaining and criticizing, or for thanksgiving and praise?

Prayer: Lord who gives me breath, You rejoice over me with singing, and I will sing to You. Help me praise You with my lips and my heart in harmony, and give me a new song in good times and hard times alike. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus receive all the glory: the focus of praise is God, not whether my singing sounds good.
Give thanks in everything: turn gratitude into a daily song, and give the glory to Jesus.
235 spiritual companions (walking the road of faith together, not alone): "speaking to one another"; praise is meant to be sung together, in one voice with our brothers and sisters.

blocks.h: This week: begin each morning with a hymn or a psalm, and invite a family member or friend to sing with you.
Quiz

quiz.q: How do many songbirds learn their songs?
o: Entirely by instinct, with no learning
By hearing adult models when young and practicing repeatedly
By watching other birds' movements
quiz.e: Like children learning to talk, many songbirds must listen, imitate, and practice.

quiz.q: What was special about the hermit thrush's song?
o: It sings only one note
Its songs are longer than human songs
Most of its pitches fall on the harmonic series, like the principle behind human scales
quiz.e: Using statistical methods, researchers found its pitches follow the simple whole-number ratios of the harmonic series.

quiz.q: According to Zephaniah 3:17, what does God do over His people?
o: Rejoices over them with joy and singing
Stays silent
Feels disappointed
quiz.e: "He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing."

units.title: A World of Color
units.sub: Three kinds of cone cells open up a world of color, and flowers hide patterns we cannot see.

share.v: For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.

blocks.h: Imagine a world of only black, white, and gray: no sky blue, no leaf green, no orange-red sunset. We see color every time we open our eyes, and we rarely stop to think what a great gift that is.
Even more amazing: the same yellow flower may carry a "bull's-eye" in a bee's eyes that we cannot see.

Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don't toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.
How do we see color?

items: Three kinds of cone cells: the human retina has three kinds of cones, most sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths of light, with absorption peaks at about 420, 534, and 564 nanometers.
The brain mixes the palette: by comparing the strength of the signals from the three kinds of cells, the brain mixes an endless variety of colors.
Color needs light: without light there is no color; an object's color is the light it reflects back.

blocks.h: The three kinds of cone cells are like three paintbrushes with only red, green, and blue paint, yet the brain, mixing them in different proportions, paints the whole world in color.

Bees and other hymenopteran insects mostly have three kinds of photoreceptors too, but in different bands: their absorption peaks lie roughly in the ultraviolet (about 340 nanometers), blue, and green, and most have no red receptor. So bees can see ultraviolet light but have trouble telling red apart.

Many petals absorb ultraviolet at the center and reflect it around the edges, forming a "bull's-eye" pattern in an insect's eyes, like a runway guiding it in to land. Field experiments show that changing this ultraviolet pattern affects how often pollinators visit.
Human color vision is based on three kinds of cone cells, with absorption peaks at short, medium, and long wavelengths.
Bee color vision includes ultraviolet receptors, and most hymenopteran insects lack red receptors.
The ultraviolet patterns of flowers affect pollinator behavior, but how strongly varies from plant to plant.
The colors of flowers, the eyes of pollinators, and the nature of light all fit together, and many see this mutual correspondence as a clue to intelligent design. This is a philosophical inference.
His wisdom and beauty: different beauty prepared for different eyes
God painted patterns on flowers for bees that humans cannot see, and prepared countless colors for humans. His beauty is more than we can see.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
We see color because there is light; we know God because He first shines on us.
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.
Go to a window or step outside, and count how many different shades of green you can see.
Reflect: Do I assume something doesn't exist just because I "can't see" it? Could God be doing work in my life that I haven't seen yet?
Prayer: Source of light, thank You for letting me see this colorful world. Open my eyes to see not only the beauty of creation, but Your works and Your heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: From man's point of view to God's point of view: I see only part; God sees the whole picture.
Relationships matter more than things: flowers and bees need each other, and in our relationships we help one another become whole.
Give thanks in everything: turn the colors we take for granted into daily reasons to give thanks.

blocks.h: This week: each day, take a photo of a color that moves you, add one line of thanks, and share it with a friend.
Quiz

quiz.q: How many kinds of cone cells in the human eye handle color vision?
o: One
Three
Six
quiz.e: The three kinds of cones are most sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths.

quiz.q: What can bees see that humans can't?
o: Ultraviolet light
Infrared light
Red
quiz.e: Bees have ultraviolet receptors, but most have no red receptor.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say about Solomon's clothing in all his glory?
o: It was more beautiful than the lilies
It was the same as the lilies
He was not dressed like one of these lilies
quiz.e: "Even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these."

units.title: The Colors of the Sky
units.sub: Blue skies, sunsets, and rainbows: poetry written by sunlight passing through the air.

share.v: I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.

blocks.h: Look up: the sky is blue. In the evening, as the sun goes down, the horizon turns orange-red and gold. After rain, a rainbow arches across the sky. These colors put on a free show every day.
Yet sunlight itself is nearly white. So where do the blue sky and the red sunset come from?
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.
Why is the sky blue?

items: Sunlight holds every color: white light is a mixture of all the colors.

Air molecules scatter light: the shorter the wavelength, the more strongly light is scattered; the strength is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength. Blue light (about 450 nanometers) is scattered about 6 times more strongly than red light (about 700 nanometers), so blue light fills the sky.
Why sunsets are red: when the sun is low, its light has to pass through much more air; the blue is scattered away along the path, leaving orange-red light to reach our eyes.

blocks.h: The atmosphere is like a sieve that specializes in "catching blue balls." When balls of every color roll through together, the blue ones are the easiest to catch and toss in every direction, so wherever you look up, you see blue. But when the path is very long, all the blue balls have been caught, and what is left is red and orange.

The British physicist Lord Rayleigh proposed this scattering law in 1871. Violet light has an even shorter wavelength, so why isn't the sky violet? The reasons include: sunlight contains less violet to begin with, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and most important, the combined response of the eye's three kinds of cones to the sky's spectrum makes us see a whitish blue.

A rainbow forms when sunlight enters raindrops, is refracted, reflects inside the drop, and is refracted again on the way out; different colors bend by different angles and spread apart. The primary bow appears with the sun at your back, on a circular arc about 42 degrees from the antisolar point, so the rainbow each person sees is really one that belongs to their own position.

The blue of a clear sky comes mainly from Rayleigh scattering, which affects short wavelengths more strongly; the red-orange of sunset comes from short wavelengths being scattered away along a longer path through the air.
That the sky looks blue rather than violet has to do with the solar spectrum, atmospheric absorption, and human color vision together.
Rainbows come from refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion in raindrops; the primary bow lies about 42 degrees from the antisolar point.

The same physical laws let sunlight pass through the atmosphere to nourish life and also paint the sky with beauty every day. Usefulness and loveliness appearing together are seen as a clue to a good Creator. This is a philosophical inference.
His goodness: the rainbow is a sign of a covenant kept
After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and every living creature that He would never again destroy the whole earth with a flood, and He set the rainbow in the clouds as its sign.
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.
Rainbows always appear after rain. God never promised there would be no more rain, but He did promise to remember His covenant in the rain.
As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh's glory.
There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at.
Find a moment today to look at the sky; if it is evening, quietly watch a whole sunset.
Reflect: What "rain" is falling in my life right now? Can I see God's covenant rainbow in the rain?
Prayer: Covenant-keeping God, Your promises never change. When I go through storms, help me look up and see the signs of Your faithfulness, and keep trusting You in hardship. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: God's promises are written in the Bible, more reliable than the weather.
From the temporary to the eternal: the rain is temporary; God's covenant is forever.
Multiplication: tell someone going through a hard time about God's faithfulness in the storm.

blocks.h: This week: write down a time you experienced God's faithfulness in difficulty, and share it this week with a friend who needs encouragement.
Quiz

quiz.q: Why is the sky blue on a clear day?
o: Because it reflects the color of the ocean
Because air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light more strongly
Because the atmosphere contains a blue gas
quiz.e: The strength of Rayleigh scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength, so more blue light is scattered.

quiz.q: Why is the sky reddish-orange at sunset?
o: Light passes through more air, and the blue is scattered away along the path
The sun's temperature drops
The clouds dye the light red
quiz.e: When the sun is low, the light's path is longer; short wavelengths are scattered away, leaving the long wavelengths.

quiz.q: God set the rainbow in the clouds as a sign of what?
o: A forecast of clearing weather
God's covenant with the earth never again to destroy it with a flood
A year of bountiful harvest
quiz.e: Genesis 9:13–15 records God's covenant.

units.title: Good Tastes
units.sub: Sweetness on the tongue and the fragrance of fruit are gifts God gave us to enjoy.

share.v: Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.

blocks.h: Bite into a perfectly ripe mango: sweet juice floods your mouth and the aroma rushes into your nose. In that moment you are experiencing an entire, finely tuned sensory system.
Eating only needs to supply energy, yet God gave food thousands of flavors and aromas.
Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food.
Taste and smell working together

items: Five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. Taste cells on the tongue each have specialized receptors; the sweet receptor, for example, is made of two proteins joined together.
Bitterness protects us: humans have more than twenty kinds of bitter receptors. Many toxic substances are bitter, and bitterness warns us to be careful.
"Flavor" is mostly in the nose: food aromas travel from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity, which is why food tastes bland when a cold blocks your nose.

blocks.h: Taste is like five basic piano keys, but smell is like an entire pipe organ. Only when the two play together do they perform a dish's rich "symphony of flavor."

In 1991 the American scientists Linda Buck and Richard Axel discovered a large family of olfactory receptor genes, for which they received the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Humans have about four hundred working olfactory receptor genes and recognize odors through combinations of different receptors.

A 2014 study estimated that people can distinguish more than a trillion odor mixtures, and it was widely reported; but other scholars soon pointed out problems with its calculation, and the true number is still unknown. What is certain is that the human nose is far more sensitive than was once thought.
The basic tastes in mammals are distinguished by different taste receptor cells on the tongue.
Olfactory receptors belong to a huge gene family, discovered in 1991.
The claim that "humans can distinguish a trillion odors" is disputed, and the actual number is still undetermined.
If eating were only for survival, food would not need to be so delicious; rich flavors and enjoyment point to a generous Creator who delights in our joy. This is a philosophical inference.
His goodness: God is glad for us to enjoy
God is not a stingy master. He created fruit "pleasant to the sight" and "good for food." The Bible says God "richly provides us with everything to enjoy."
...but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.
Just as the body's tongue can taste sweetness, the spiritual life can also "taste" God's goodness: knowing Him through experience.
Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.
How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth!
At your next meal, close your eyes as you take the first bite, savor it slowly, and name three flavors you taste.
Reflect: Have I only "heard" that God is good, or have I personally "tasted" His goodness?

Prayer: God who richly provides everything, thank You for giving me the ability to taste, to smell, and to enjoy. Help me enjoy not only Your gifts but You, the Giver, and taste the sweetness of Your Word every day. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The order of relationships: first enjoy God, then enjoy what God gives; don't let the gift replace the Giver.
Give thanks in everything: grace before meals is not a formality; it acknowledges that everything comes from Him.
People matter more than tasks: good food is best shared, and one meal can build a relationship.

blocks.h: This week: invite a friend or neighbor for a meal. Give thanks together before eating, and afterward share one experience of "tasting the Lord's goodness."
Quiz

quiz.q: Why does food taste bland when a cold blocks your nose?
o: Because the taste buds on your tongue stop working
Because the food itself has become weaker
Because much of food's "flavor" comes from smell
quiz.e: Food aromas travel from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity; with a blocked nose, much of that information is lost.

quiz.q: What is the current status of the claim that "humans can distinguish a trillion odors"?
o: Widely confirmed
Disputed; the actual number is still unclear
Proven that humans can distinguish only ten odors
quiz.e: The 2014 estimate was soon shown to have methodological problems, and the true number remains undetermined.

quiz.q: How does 1 Timothy 6:17 describe God?
o: The God who richly provides us with everything to enjoy
A God who only wants us to suffer
A God who doesn't care about people
quiz.e: "...on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy."

units.title: Why Are We Moved by Beauty?
units.sub: Beauty is not merely a survival tool; it is God's gift and a signpost on the road home.

share.v: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.

blocks.h: Before a magnificent starry sky, a moving melody, or a baby's smile, people hold their breath, shed tears, and fall speechless. Where does this feeling come from?
Sometimes beauty brings not only joy but an indescribable longing, as if beauty were pointing to somewhere farther away.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts.
Is a sense of beauty a survival necessity?

items: Universal: every human culture has music, decoration, and art.
Intense: experiences of beauty activate the brain's reward system and bring real bodily responses, like goosebumps.
Beyond need: appreciating a symphony or a starry sky is hard to trade directly for food or safety.

blocks.h: Beauty is like an unsigned letter in familiar handwriting. As you read it, someone comes to mind. Beauty itself is not the sender, but it makes you think of the One who sent it.

The biologist Richard Prum argues that many beautiful traits in animals may have been selected simply because they were liked, not necessarily because they helped survival; his theory has stirred much discussion among scholars. At the very least, it shows that explaining beauty only in terms of "helping survival" is not easy.

In "The Weight of Glory," C. S. Lewis says that the longing beauty awakens in us is like the scent of a flower we have not yet found, the echo of a tune we have not yet heard; beauty itself is not what we truly long for, but news that comes to us through beauty.

items.h: A sense of beauty may come from sexual selection, or from preferences for healthy, safe environments (such as water sources and open views). These explanations have some evidence, but there is still much debate.
Humans can appreciate beauty because they are made in the image of God, and God Himself is the source of beauty and goodness. The sense of beauty is a gift and a clue pointing to God.
Many Christian scholars hold that science describing "how" our sense of beauty works does not rule out "why" God gave it.

blocks.h: Music, decoration, and art are found in every human culture.
Intense experiences of beauty (such as the chills music brings) are linked with activity in the brain's reward system.
There are several hypotheses for the evolutionary origin of the sense of beauty, including sexual selection and environmental preferences; none is settled.
Our longing for beauty exceeds what any created thing can satisfy; one of the most reasonable explanations is that we were made for One who is supremely beautiful. This is a philosophical inference.
His beauty: every good thing comes from Him

Snowflakes, peacocks, butterflies, birdsong, colors, sunsets, and delicious food are all gifts coming down from "the Father of lights." However good a gift is, its purpose is to bring us to the One who gave it.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
The deepest beauty is not in a landscape but on the cross: the most beautiful Lord gave Himself for us.
You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
But as it is written, "Things which an eye didn't see, and an ear didn't hear, which didn't enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him."
Think back over the eight units of this hall, pick the scene that moved you most, and bring it into prayer.
Reflect: Have I stopped at the gift, or have I followed the gift to find the God who gave it?

Prayer: Father of lights, every good thing comes from You. Thank You for placing beauty in the world and eternity in my heart. Help me not to stop at created things, but through them to love You more, and to gaze on Your beauty all my life. In Jesus' name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: good things are servants, not masters; let Jesus take first place in my heart.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: every time beauty moves me, give the thanks and glory to Him.
Build God's kingdom system: in family, church, and work, display God's goodness and beauty through good words and deeds.

blocks.h: This week: do one "beautiful and good thing" this week, such as preparing a thoughtful meal for your family or writing a thank-you card, and quietly offer it to God in your heart.

Congratulations on completing the Beauty Hall! From snowflakes, peacocks, and butterflies to birdsong, color, the sky, and taste, you have seen a God who is not only powerful but beautiful and good. May you gaze on His beauty all your life, and live out His goodness.
Quiz

quiz.q: According to this unit, what is our sense of beauty like?
o: Only about survival, with no other meaning
Universal, intense, and often beyond what survival requires
Found in only a few cultures
quiz.e: The sense of beauty is universal and brings intense responses, yet it is hard to explain fully by survival needs.

quiz.q: What did C. S. Lewis compare the longing beauty brings to?
o: The scent of a flower we have not yet found
A wonderful dinner
A promotion notice
quiz.e: Beauty itself is not what we truly long for, but news that comes to us through beauty.

quiz.q: According to James 1:17, where does every good gift come from?
o: From human effort
From good luck
Coming down from the Father of lights
quiz.e: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights."

questions.q: Why is the world not only functional but so beautiful?
Why are people moved by beauty, and even long for something more beautiful?
